payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
The Drift Was Never the Interesting Part

¶1 I want to start with a morning in late January, two winters ago, because it is the morning people imagine when they hear that I ride a bicycle to work all year. It was eleven below zero at the bridge, cold enough that the chain ticked like a cooling engine, and the river path had not been plowed. I walked the bike a mile and a half through shin-deep snow and arrived at the clinic forty minutes late. That is the picture: a stubborn woman dragging a machine through a drift. I am here tonight to tell you that the picture is accurate and that it is also almost entirely beside the point.

¶2 Of the roughly one hundred and twenty working days between November and March, that morning was one of perhaps four I would call genuinely bad. The others were simply cold, which is a different thing. Cold is a problem of clothing; snow is a problem of maintenance; and only the first of these is mine to solve. When I say winter commuting, I do not mean an expedition. I mean a twenty-two-minute ride on studded tires, a pair of mittens that cost less than a tank of gasoline, and a path that somebody has cleared. Remove that last item and the whole arrangement collapses, not because the riders are weak but because nobody can pedal through a foot of unplowed snow, any more than you can drive through it.

¶3 I know what some of you are thinking, because I have heard it at this forum before: that the riders are a handful of enthusiasts, and that a city of thirty thousand cannot justify a plow for a few dozen people in reflective jackets. It is a fair objection, and I want to take it seriously rather than wave it away. The count is low because the path is unreliable, and the path is unreliable because the count is low; the city has built itself a circle and then pointed at the circle as proof. Last winter, when Public Works kept the path cleared for six weeks as a trial, the counter at the Hollis Street bridge recorded an average of ninety-one riders a day, up from nineteen the year before. Nobody bought new bicycles in February. Those riders were already here, waiting for the city to decide whether they existed.

¶4 Consider how we treat the sidewalk. We do not ask whether enough people walk on Fenwick Avenue in January to justify shoveling it; we assume that a sidewalk under snow is a failure of the city, not a verdict on pedestrians. A bicycle path is a sidewalk with a longer stride. It carries the nurse, the night-shift baker, the ninth-grader too young to drive whose parents both leave the house before seven. Those people do not stop needing to get across town when the temperature drops; they simply stop being counted.

¶5 Let me be honest about the limits of what I am asking. There will be mornings, four or five a winter, when the plow cannot keep up and nobody should be on the path, and I am not asking the city to promise otherwise. I am asking for something smaller and duller: that the river path go on the same plowing schedule as the residential streets, which by Public Works' own estimate would add about eleven thousand dollars a year to a snow budget of just under two million. That is less than the cost of one of the salt trucks parked behind this building.

¶6 So here is the picture I would rather you carry out of this room tonight. Not a woman hauling a bicycle through a drift, but a cleared path at seven in the morning, a few tail-lights blinking red against the snow, the baker and the nurse and the ninth-grader going to work in the ordinary way, in a town that decided they were worth a plow. The drift was never the interesting part. The interesting part is what the town does about it.

ALTON original passage
Sixty-One Sycamores

¶1 When I was twenty-three and newly hired by the town of Harrow Fen, my supervisor handed me a clipboard and told me to count the trees on Calder Avenue. I assumed it was busywork. It took four days, because every sycamore on that street had something to say: a hollow where a raccoon had raised three litters, a lightning scar healed over like a closed eye, a root that had lifted a sidewalk slab and then, with a patience I did not yet understand, grown around it. Graduates, I have been asked to speak to you about your futures, and I intend to, but I am going to do it by talking about those sycamores, because last Tuesday the council voted to widen Calder Avenue, and the plan calls for removing all sixty-one of them.

¶2 Let me be precise about what we mean when we say old-growth on a city street, since the phrase was borrowed from forestry and does not fit perfectly. In a forest, old growth describes a stand that has never been cleared. On a street, it describes something rarer: a tree that has survived a century of paving, trenching, salt, and committees. Every one of those sycamores was planted by a person who knew they would never sit in its shade. That is not sentiment; that is the definition.

¶3 You have spent years learning to call things by their proper names, so call a street tree what it is: infrastructure. A storm sewer carries water away; a mature sycamore intercepts roughly three thousand gallons of rainfall a year before it ever reaches the sewer. A transformer cools a block in August; the canopy on Calder lowers surface temperature by double digits, according to the thermal survey our own department commissioned seven years ago. We do not demolish a bridge because it is old. We inspect it, we repair it, and when we must, we close a lane. Yet the same council that budgets forty years of maintenance for a culvert will vote to erase a hundred and forty years of canopy in an afternoon, because a tree, unlike a culvert, does not appear on the balance sheet as an asset that depreciates.

¶4 I will concede the obvious. Some old trees must come down. I have signed the removal orders myself, standing under a red oak with a fungal rot that had eaten two-thirds of its heartwood, and I did not sleep well afterward, but I signed. A dangerous tree is not a monument; it is a liability with leaves. But the Calder sycamores are not dangerous. The widening is proposed so that traffic can move eleven seconds faster at the Pell Street light. Eleven seconds. We are being asked to trade a century for a fraction of a minute, and to call the trade progress.

¶5 So here is what I am asking of you, and it is harder than it sounds. You will be the ones in the room when the next Calder Avenue comes up for a vote. You will have the drawings, the models, the cost estimates, and you will be tempted to treat a mature tree the way the software treats it: as a circle on a plan, easily erased and easily redrawn somewhere else. Resist that. A sapling planted in mitigation is not a replacement; it is an IOU that will not be paid during your career, or your children's. Insist that the removal of an old-growth street tree be justified the way we justify closing a hospital wing: reluctantly, publicly, and with the arithmetic on the table.

¶6 I counted sixty-one sycamores in my first week of work. I would like to count them again at the end of yours. Go and be the kind of planners who make that possible.

The Hand That Drew It: Remembering Teodora Quist

¶1 Teodora Quist kept a jar of eraser crumbs on her drafting table and told every new apprentice that it was the most honest record of her career. She died last month in Lower Marrow at eighty-one, in the house behind the county survey office where she had drawn maps for forty-three years. She taught a generation of us that a map is not a picture of the world. It is a case made about the world, built with the same tools as any other case: selection, emphasis, and omission.

¶2 Most people would say a map is a drawing that shows where things are. Quist would say it is a drawing that shows which things the mapmaker decided you should know are there. A sheet of paper cannot hold a county; it holds perhaps a thousandth of what a county contains, and the rest must be left off. Every blank space, she liked to say, is a verdict. The road drawn thick and the stream drawn thin, the village named and the settlement unnamed, the boundary inked solid and the boundary left dotted: these are not observations but rulings.

¶3 The clearest demonstration came when the Marrow County Board asked her office for a map to accompany a vote on building along the river's lower terrace. Standard practice would have been to shade the floodplain in the pale blue the state style guide recommended, a blue so gentle it reads as decoration. Quist shaded it in a mud brown no one could mistake for ornament, and she printed the crest of the 1961 flood at every bridge. The developers' attorney called the map inflammatory. She answered that the pale blue was also inflammatory; it simply inflamed in the other direction. The board voted nine to two against the project, and three members later said the brown was what they remembered when they voted.

¶4 Her critics, and she had them, said this proved she was an advocate who happened to own a drafting pen rather than a surveyor who happened to have opinions. I will grant them half of that. She did want the project stopped, and she said so to anyone who asked. But the charge assumes that somewhere a map exists with no advocate behind it, a sheet that merely reports, and in forty-three years she never saw one and neither have I. The pale blue floodplain had an advocate too; he was just quieter about it. What distinguished Quist was not that her maps argued but that she signed the argument.

¶5 She trained apprentices with a single exercise, repeated until it became reflex. Given one set of survey data for a single square mile, we drew three maps: one for a family thinking of buying a house there, one for a company planning a pipeline, and one for a child who would walk to school along its lanes. The data never changed. The maps never matched. The buyer's map grew contour lines and drainage; the pipeline's map grew easements and bedrock; the child's map grew crossings, dogs, and the one hedge you could cut through. After the third round, nobody could say "just the facts" with a straight face, which was, I think, the whole point.

¶6 The week after she died I went to the survey office, mostly to sit in the chair, and the jar of eraser crumbs was still there, fuller than I remembered. It struck me that she had kept it because it was, in its way, her finest map: a record of every line she had chosen, on reflection, not to let stand. We will mourn her, and we will do it properly. But I would ask anyone reading this, the next time a map is unfolded at a council meeting or on a phone screen, to do what she did and look first for the hand that drew it. Ask what it was told to show you. Then ask what it was told to leave out.

The Clipboard and the Box: On Counting the Uncountable

¶1 The morning of the Pellam Hollow winter count began, as it has for the eleven years I have taken part, with a thermos, a clipboard, and an argument about whether the bird on the wire was a house finch or a purple finch. It was a house finch. By noon our team of four had recorded sixty-one species, mis-tallied a flock of starlings at least twice, and lost one volunteer to a warm car. I mention this not to be charming but because Halvard Teague's new book, Counting the Uncountable, takes mornings like mine as its target, and it is only fair to admit at the outset that I am one of the people he is counting against.

¶2 Teague, a population ecologist who built survey models for two decades before turning to write for a general audience, has produced a lucid, impatient, and frequently persuasive book. His thesis is simple: the great amateur bird counts that have run each winter for more than a century yield data so uneven that the trends drawn from them are closer to folklore than to measurement. Volunteers vary in skill, in stamina, and in honesty with themselves. Routes drift from year to year. A count conducted by forty people in a mild December cannot be laid beside a count conducted by nine people in a blizzard and called a comparison. Teague writes with the controlled exasperation of a man who has spent years cleaning other people's spreadsheets, and the chapters in which he does the cleaning in front of us are the best in the book.

¶3 I would like to report that he is wrong about the numbers, but he is not. He reanalyzes a regional tally and finds that correcting for observer effort alone shrinks a celebrated forty percent decline in a woodland sparrow to something nearer twelve, with error bars wide enough to swallow the result entirely. I have been on routes where the cold ended the day early, and I have seen the same cardinal counted by two teams who met at a fence line and did not compare notes. Anyone who has held the clipboard knows that the tally is an estimate wearing the costume of a fact.

¶4 And yet the book has a hole at its center, and the hole is the word knowledge. Teague uses it to mean one thing only, a number stable enough to publish, and having defined it so narrowly, he concludes that an enterprise which produces unstable numbers produces nothing. But a count is not a measuring instrument that happens to be operated by people; it is a people-making instrument that happens to produce a measurement. What it manufactures, reliably and in quantity, is observers.

¶5 Consider my neighbor Dorrit, a retired bus mechanic who joined our team six winters ago because his daughter had moved away and the house was quiet. The first year he could not tell a chickadee from a nuthatch; by the third he was correcting me on the call of a brown creeper; by the fifth he had noticed that the creek behind the gravel yard, which he had driven past for thirty years, had gone silent of kingfishers, and he went to the town meeting to ask why. The meeting led to a water test, the test to a finding, and the finding to a culvert being replaced. No model counted that. Teague would say, correctly, that Dorrit's kingfisher observation is an anecdote and not a trend, and he would be missing the point: the count did not give us a trend, it gave us Dorrit, and Dorrit gave us the culvert.

¶6 The book's final chapter proposes a remedy, and it is here that Teague's narrowness becomes almost comic. He would replace the volunteers with acoustic sensors, weatherproof boxes that listen all winter and identify calls by software, and he is probably right that the boxes would produce cleaner data. They would also produce no Dorrits. A town that outsources its listening to a box on a pole will have excellent records of the birds it is no longer able to hear. Read Counting the Uncountable for its chapters on method, which are the sharpest explanation of survey bias I have encountered in plain prose; then go out in December with a clipboard anyway, and count badly, and become someone who notices.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
A Fence Around an Hour

¶1 The pledge card came in the same envelope as the library's autumn newsletter, printed on oatmeal-colored stock with a line for each member of the household to sign. "Screens Down at Supper," it read, and underneath, in smaller type, "Give your children back the table." I read it twice at my own kitchen table, phone face down beside the sugar bowl, and felt the particular unease of someone who agrees with a proposal and distrusts its wording. Give the children back the table? Who, exactly, had taken it from them?

¶2 My grandmother, Solveig Arnesen, bought her first radio in the autumn of 1938, a walnut cabinet set that cost her, according to the household ledger she kept in a looping hand, thirty-one dollars and forty cents. The ledger records the purchase on a Tuesday. By the following Sunday a second entry appears, not a sum but a sentence: "No set from six to seven. All of us." The family story is that my grandfather, not the children, had been the trouble, sitting with his ear to the speaker through an entire meal while the program crackled about grain prices and a prizefight in a city none of them would ever see. The rule she wrote was not a punishment for the young. It was a fence she built around an hour, and she built it to keep herself and her husband inside as much as anyone.

¶3 The pattern repeated itself with a regularity that would be comic if it were not so instructive. In 1954 the telephone arrived, and my mother remembers the cord unplugged at a quarter to six and coiled on top of the icebox like a sleeping cat. In 1967 the television came, and with it a new entry in a new ledger, this time in my mother's hand: "Set off at supper, no exceptions, Dad included." Each machine was a stranger at the door, and each time the household did the same thing: it did not bar the stranger, it told the stranger when to call. The radio stayed; the telephone stayed; the television, heaven help us, stayed. What changed was that a single hour was marked off as belonging to the people at the table rather than to the voices coming through the wall.

¶4 There is a difference, I think, between a curfew and a ritual, and the difference matters more than the hour chosen. A curfew is a rule imposed on someone by someone else; it names a suspect and a warden. A ritual is a thing a group does together, on purpose, at a set time, because doing it together is the point. The mill at the foot of Carrow Bend used to blow its whistle at noon, and nobody heard that whistle as an accusation; it was simply the sound of everyone stopping at once. My grandmother's "All of us" was a whistle, not a warrant.

¶5 I will concede that the ledgers do not record a single happy supper. They record cabbage and coal and the price of shoes, and the surviving letters mention more than one meal eaten in a silence that was sullen rather than peaceful, teenagers and tired parents with nothing to say and a forbidden radio in the next room. Nostalgia would have me believe that the quiet hour produced conversation; the evidence suggests only that it produced attendance. But attendance, it turns out, is not nothing. The sullen suppers of 1941 are the ones my mother still describes in detail, down to the pattern on the oilcloth, and she cannot describe a single evening when the set was on.

¶6 So I will sign the card, and I would urge you to sign it as well, though I would ask you to take a pen and cross out the second line before you do. Do not give the children back the table. Sit down at it yourself, phone in the drawer, and let them see you, every night, until the hour belongs to all of you and nobody remembers whom it was meant to protect. My grandmother knew this in 1938 with a radio she could barely afford. The machine has changed. The fence has not.

What the Spreadsheet Cannot Hear

¶1 The memo arrived on a Tuesday, between a boiler quote and a reminder that my van inspection was overdue. The board, it said, is considering ending the ride-along program, which pairs first-year apprentices with a retired member for two days a month, and replacing it with a library of training videos. The videos, the memo assured us, would be professionally produced. I have no doubt that they would be. I also have no doubt that they would be a mistake, and I would like to explain why before the vote next month.

¶2 When I was nineteen I rode along with Augie Pell, who had been sweating copper since before I was born and who did not, as far as I could tell, approve of me. On my third day he stopped in a basement in Fenwick Heights, laid his palm against a supply line, and asked me what I heard. I heard nothing. He said that was the problem: the line was humming, faintly, and the hum meant a loose strap upstream that would, in a year or two, wear a hole through the pipe. He did not show me where the strap was; he made me stand there with my own hand on the pipe until I could feel what he felt, which took most of the afternoon and all of my pride.

¶3 There is a kind of knowledge that can be written down, and the trades are full of it: clearances, torque values, the order in which you open valves. A video carries that knowledge perfectly well. But there is another kind of knowledge that lives only in a person, and it is the kind that separates a plumber from someone who owns plumbing tools. It is the habit of noticing: the faint hum, the smell of flux mixed wrong, the way a homeowner's voice changes when the leak she describes is not the one she is worried about. No camera records a habit. A habit is transferred the way Augie transferred it, by standing next to someone long enough that his attention starts to shape yours.

¶4 I will grant the board its arithmetic. The program costs roughly 40,000 dollars a year, it reaches perhaps thirty apprentices, and some of our retired members are, to put it gently, set in their ways. A video library would cost less, reach everyone, and never tell an apprentice that her generation does not know how to work. But the expense that looks like waste on the spreadsheet is the whole point. What we are paying for is hours in basements, because time is the only medium in which attention passes from one pair of hands to another. Cut the hours and you have not made the program efficient; you have removed the thing it was for.

¶5 I should admit something the memo does not mention: the traffic on those ride-alongs does not run in one direction. Last spring I rode along myself, as the elder this time, with Teo Marsh, twenty-two, who carried a tablet the way I carry a pipe wrench. On our second job he pulled up a thermal image of a wall and found, in four minutes, a slab leak I had planned to hunt all morning with a listening rod. I was annoyed, and then I was grateful, and then I asked him to show me how the thing worked. He was patient with me, which is more than I can say for Augie. The retired members are not only being preserved by this program; they are being updated.

¶6 So here is what I am asking. Come to the meeting on the fourteenth, and when the board presents its cost per apprentice, ask whether the number counts the pipes that did not burst or the old plumbers who learned to read a thermal camera. You will not get an answer; nobody has one. That is not a flaw in the program. It is a description of what it does.

Who Wrote the English Sentences

¶1 Last Tuesday the Ambervale Prize announced its shortlist, and the press release named six novels, six authors, and six publishers, but not one translator. Four of those six books were written in languages the jury does not read. I know this because I translated one of them. My name appears on page four of the paperback, in a typeface smaller than the one used to describe the paper stock.

¶2 Readers sometimes imagine translation as a kind of plumbing: the words flow in one end of the pipe in Norwegian and come out the other end in English, and the translator merely checks for leaks. The image is comforting, and it is wrong. A sentence in one language is not a container with a fixed amount of meaning inside it; it is a set of choices that a second language cannot reproduce but can only answer. When the Norwegian novelist Sigrun Aalvik wrote that her heroine "went out into the weather," she used a verb that in her dialect also means to quarrel. English has no such verb. I had to decide whether the woman walked into a storm or into an argument, and whichever I chose, the English reader would believe the author had chosen it.

¶3 Consider the scale of the problem. Aalvik's novel runs to roughly ninety thousand words, and I made, by my own rough count, something near forty decisions a page that no dictionary could make for me: where to break a sentence, which of three possible synonyms carried the right chill, whether a joke survived or had to be replaced with a different joke. Multiply that by three hundred pages and you arrive at an English book that shares a plot and a spirit with the Norwegian one but shares none of its sentences. Every sentence the English reader admires, I wrote. Every sentence the reader finds clumsy, I also wrote.

¶4 I can hear the objection, because I have made it myself at dinner parties: the story, the characters, the architecture of the book belong to Aalvik, and the translator is at most a skilled carpenter working from her drawings. There is something to this. I did not invent the heroine, and I would not want credit for her. But a carpenter who selects every board, every joint, and every finish, and whose work the client lives inside for years, is not usually left off the plaque. Architecture is credited; so is the building.

¶5 Why, then, does the convention of the invisible translator persist? Partly because publishers fear that a second name on the cover warns the buyer that the book is foreign, and foreign, in the sales meeting, means difficult. Partly because reviewers, who seldom read the original, find it easier to praise "the author's luminous prose" than to admit they are praising prose whose author they cannot identify. And partly, I confess, because translators themselves have cultivated a monkish modesty, as though visibility were a kind of vanity. The effect is circular: because we are unnamed, we seem unimportant, and because we seem unimportant, nobody thinks to name us.

¶6 I am not asking for the author's name to be removed, or shrunk, or shared with mine in some awkward hyphenated compound. I am asking for a line of type on the front of the book, the same size as the blurb from a novelist nobody has heard of, that says who wrote the English sentences. If you run a prize, name the translator in the press release. If you review books, say which words you are actually quoting. And if you are a reader who has ever loved a novel written in a language you do not speak, you have already loved a translator's work; you simply were not told whom to thank.

[1] Good evening, members of the Larkhaven City Council. [2] My name is Odile Strand, and I have lived on Quarry Hill Road for twenty-two years. [3] Tonight I want to talk about lights.

[4] Every second Saturday, the Larkhaven Stargazers Club sets up telescopes in the gravel lot behind the public library. [9] The Cutler Avenue fixtures are uncovered globes that throw about a third of their light sideways and upward, where it lights nothing but the sky. [10] The town of Fenwick Ridge, forty miles north, replaced its globes with fully shielded fixtures and reported that its electricity bill for street lighting dropped by 18 percent. [11] Shielded fixtures, which aim light downward toward the street, they cost about the same as the globes the city currently uses and they also last just as long as the globes do.

[12] Anyway, that is basically all I have got, so thanks for listening to me ramble.

paragraphs: Good evening, members of the Larkhaven City Council.
My name is Odile Strand, and I have lived on Quarry Hill Road for twenty-two years.

The Cutler Avenue fixtures are uncovered globes that throw about a third of their light sideways and upward, where it lights nothing but the sky.
The town of Fenwick Ridge, forty miles north, replaced its globes with fully shielded fixtures and reported that its electricity bill for street lighting dropped by 18 percent.
